title: Authentication decorator fails open when authentication aborts
description: require_auth catches every Exception, including the abort(401) it raises when no valid bearer token is present, logs it, sets g.user to None, and then invokes the protected view anyway. Protected handlers that do not immediately dereference g.user can therefore be reached without authentication, while others produce an internal error instead of a 401.
evidence: Lines 52-58 catch abort/other exceptions and unconditionally return f(*args, **kwargs). A request without credentials to GET /account reaches the view and returns HTTP 500 rather than 401, demonstrating that the authentication failure is swallowed.

title: Order details are exposed without ownership authorization
description: The authenticated order detail route calls get_order directly rather than own_order. get_order checks only whether the order exists and does not compare customer_id with the requesting user, so any caller can read another customer's order, line items, and refunds. Due to the failing authentication decorator, unauthenticated callers can also reach this route.
evidence: show_order at lines 46-49 returns order_json(get_order(order_id)); the ownership check exists separately in own_order at lines 32-36 but is not used. GET /orders/1 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and the complete order including SKU, prices, and refund data.

title: Refresh endpoint accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied token with verify_signature=False, then trusts its sub claim to select a real user and issues a newly signed token. An attacker can construct an unsigned token naming any user ID and obtain a valid session token for that account without knowing the signing secret.
evidence: Lines 101-107 explicitly disable signature verification and call make_token for the loaded sub. POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned token containing {"sub":1} returned HTTP 200 and a freshly signed bearer token.

title: JWT signing key is hardcoded in source
description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed, repository-visible string. Anyone who obtains the source or a deployment artifact can forge HS256 tokens for arbitrary user IDs and roles, bypassing authentication and staff authorization.
evidence: config.py line 3 sets SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d"; auth.py lines 27 and 42 use it for all JWT signing and verification.

title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
description: Password hashing uses a single unsalted SHA-256 digest with no work factor or password-hashing scheme. A database disclosure enables efficient offline dictionary and brute-force cracking, and identical passwords produce identical hashes.
evidence: hash_password at lines 15-16 is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(), and registration stores that value at line 78.

title: Admin review report builds SQL with a user-controlled display name
description: The reviews report interpolates customer.display_name directly into a SQL string. Display names are set by customers through the account update endpoint, so a customer can store quote/SQL syntax and trigger SQL injection when staff request the report for that customer.
evidence: admin.py lines 78-80 construct f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC". The value originates from auth.py lines 119-125, where any authenticated user can update display_name.
